title: Quantization reproducibility and KV-cache / seed interaction workshop
summary: Deep technical session to reproduce and diagnose small but material accuracy regressions observed after INT8/GPTQ rollout. Focus on how random seeds, KV cache warmup, batching, and deterministic kernels (cuDNN/TF32) interact on both hosted and Nexora's on-prem VPC. Agreed action items: run seeded repro harness, collect full per-layer logits diffs, share quantization config and kernel build IDs, schedule follow-up with deterministic staging run.
action_items: Luis Romero (Redwood SE): Provide a deterministic repro harness (Docker + pinned CUDA/cuDNN) and a script to replay failing prompts; due 2026-10-06
Tom Nguyen (Nexora): Share 200 failing prompts and the model checkpoint identifiers + seed used during local quantization; due 2026-10-04
Arjun Patel (Redwood SRE) & Priya Patel (Nexora Infra): Coordinate an on-prem staging run with identical kernel versions and CPU affinity settings; tentative date 2026-10-08
Sara Lim (Nexora): Run per-layer output diffs (logits) for the small test set and upload to shared benchmark sheet link; due 2026-10-05
next_steps: Redwood to drop deterministic docker image and runbook
Customer to run the harness and attach seed/quant logs
Joint on-prem run to confirm if KV cache warmup order is causing non-determinism
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-09-29
- Time: 15:00 PT
- Duration: 54 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Luis Romero (Redwood SE); Arjun Patel (Redwood SRE); Tom Nguyen (Nexora ML Eng); Priya Patel (Nexora Infra Lead); Sara Lim (Nexora DS); Rajesh Menon (Nexora Security)

Auto-summary (auto): group discussed quantization regressions, reproducibility, kernels, KV cache interactions.

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick agenda — reproduce the regression, identify whether it's quantization (GPTQ/AWQ) or runtime (kv/batching/kernels) and next steps.
00:18 Tom Nguyen: Thanks, yeah we've seen a consistent ~0.8-1.2% drop on our ROUGE-ish metric after we pushed INT8+GPTQ in the canary. It's small but product flagged it.
00:32 Maya Chen: Got it. Can you confirm the environment — on-prem GPU type, CUDA/cuDNN versions, and whether you used our hosted artifacts or built locally?
00:45 Tom Nguyen: We're on A100s, but we built GPTQ locally with a patched quant lib — used CUDA 11.8 and cuDNN 8.4, and we ran quantization with seed 7. We also tried seed 42 and saw different diffs.
01:02 Luis Romero: (interrupts) When you say different diffs — do you mean different seeds change the final accuracy after quantizing? Are we talking about stochastic rounding or pruning randomness during GPTQ retraining?
01:18 Tom Nguyen: Yeah, a bit of both. Our GPTQ flow reorders some micro-batches during per-layer calibration and there's a stochastic element in the optimizer. With seed 7 we saw less degradation than seed 42, but not consistently.
01:35 Priya Patel: Also worth noting our inference job uses persistent KV cache and prefix caching; sometimes cold starts warm up differently depending on request ordering.
01:48 Sara Lim: We also saw the largest deltas on long-sequence summarization prompts — sequences ~2048 tokens. Shorter prompts are fine.
02:05 Luis Romero: That points at two interacting things: quantization-induced numeric drift across layers and KV cache ordering/caching behavior that may amplify small differences. If the kv cache warmup order changes, caches will store different key/values and subsequent tokens drift.
02:22 Rajesh Menon: From security we need to know if deterministic builds are possible. For audits, reproducibility helps.
02:34 Maya Chen: Absolutely. Luis, can you walk through how we'd do a deterministic repro on Redwood's side?
02:40 Luis Romero: Sure. We'll provide a docker image with pinned CUDA/cuDNN, pinned MKL/OpenBLAS, and our runtime built with deterministic flags where possible. Then supply a small harness: fixed seed, fixed thread affinity, pinned kernel selection (we'll log kernel IDs). That lets us see if discrepancies are from quantization or the runtime.
03:05 Tom Nguyen: That would help. Right now our internal test harness wasn't capturing per-layer logits, only final token-level outputs.
03:15 Luis Romero: We should capture raw logits and per-layer max absolute diff and relative diff. Also capture KV cache snapshots at layer boundaries — even simple checksums can show divergence points.
03:29 Sara Lim: Are there known layers that are particularly sensitive? We've seen the mid transformer layers (like layers 10-18 on our 24-layer model) show the most movement.
03:40 Luis Romero: Yep that's common. Middle layers often carry the attention mixing dynamics; small perturbations amplify. GPTQ/AWQ differences — AWQ sometimes keeps more outlier ranges which helps. For INT8 we also care about per-channel scaling and dynamic range.
03:56 Maya Chen: Can you explain in plain terms the AWQ vs GPTQ tradeoff we should consider?
04:02 Luis Romero: Sure — GPTQ is quantization-aware post-training with per-layer calibration and sometimes per-channel, tends to be more accurate but slower to compute. AWQ is a more aggressive weight-quant method with heuristics that preserve some outliers and tries to be faster. AWQ can be less stable across seeds if the calibration set is small.
04:28 Tom Nguyen: We used AWQ for faster iteration. Might be the calibration set size: we used 512 calibration examples with long sequences which may bias scalings.
04:39 Maya Chen: Okay so hypothesis A: calibration set + seed -> different scaling factors -> small per-layer drift -> KV cache warmup order amplifies -> output delta for long sequences. Hypothesis B: runtime non-determinism (cuDNN kernel selection, fused kernels with nondeterministic reductions) is the main cause.
05:02 Priya Patel: Our ops team also noted differences when we toggle TF32/FP32 math modes — could that be relevant for FP8 vs INT8 paths?
05:12 Luis Romero: Yes. On some kernels TF32/TF32 heuristics alter accumulation and make traces nondeterministic. We need to pin math modes during the repro run. Also some fused attention kernels in upstream lib are nondeterministic across thread scheduling.
05:31 Tom Nguyen: Is there a quick check to see whether it's quantization vs runtime?
05:36 Luis Romero: Run quantized model with float emulation (simulate INT8 by applying quant/dequant in fp32 deterministically) and compare to locally-quantized binary model. If the emulation reproduces drift, it's quantization; if not, it's likely runtime.
05:55 Maya Chen: Good, we'll provide emulation tools.
05:59 (short pause)
06:10 Sara Lim: One more wrinkle — we saw differences only when batch size > 1 and with request sharding. Single-request runs are stable.
06:20 Luis Romero: That suggests batching and KV coalescing order matter. When you batch, the request ordering for KV writes can be different depending on scheduler, which changes cache contents.
06:32 Tom Nguyen: So if we can reproduce with batch size 1 consistently, it's likely scheduling/kv ordering. But our production uses batch size 4 for perf.
06:44 Arjun Patel: For the on-prem stage we'll enforce a single-threaded run to see if threading interleaves are the cause.
06:52 Maya Chen: Let's talk data to collect — Tom, please share failing prompts and the quant config. Luis, you'll supply the deterministic docker and kernel logging. Arjun and Priya coordinate environment parity.
07:05 Tom Nguyen: I'll upload the prompt set and config — note we used layerwise smooth quant but enabled bias folding.
07:15 Luis Romero: Noted; bias folding can change per-channel dynamics. We'll instrument bias folding logs.
07:22 Sara Lim: Any chance this is due to KV cache staleness — like when we switch to a canary model mid-session?
07:30 Maya Chen: Good point — we need to check rollout logic. If requests span a model switch, caches are incompatible.
07:39 Priya Patel: Our rollout uses sticky sessions but there might be edge cases. We'll audit sticky session logs for timestamped model hashes.
07:50 Tom Nguyen: On the quant side, is there a way to pin AWQ/GPTQ calibration to remove stochastic training? We can run GPTQ with fixed minibatch order and seed, but the implementation does random shuffle by default.
08:04 Luis Romero: Yes, run with deterministic shuffle and fixed RNG. We'll include that in the harness. Also remove any layerwise dropout and disable cuBLAS autotune flags.
08:18 Rajesh Menon: Are we exposing any customer data through calibration samples? Need to ensure calibration corpus is scrubbed.
08:25 Sara Lim: We'll provide synthetic or redacted prompts for the repro set.
08:30 Maya Chen: Perfect. I want to dig into a concrete reproduction plan. Step 1: Redwood provides a container with pinned libs, kernel logging, and a script that runs emulated quant (fp32 with quant/dequant) and binary quant in the same env. Step 2: Nexora runs both single-request and batched-request runs with provided prompts and seeds. Step 3: Both teams compare per-layer diffs and KV checksums to find divergence point.
09:02 Luis Romero: We'll also include a small tool to snapshot KV cache (hash per layer per step) so you can see exactly when caches diverge.
09:12 Tom Nguyen: Awesome. Regarding FP8 — we briefly explored FP8 for latency but worried about range/overflow and deterministic accumulators. Is FP8 actually more stable for us?
09:26 Luis Romero: FP8 can be more forgiving for distribution shift because it keeps a floating exponent, but it also has a smaller dynamic range per block and relies heavily on scaling and exponent bias. On GPU, FP8 paths may use different kernels and sometimes mixed precision accumulation which again can be non-deterministic. For reproducibility, INT8 with deterministic quant/dequant is easier to reason about, but FP8 can yield better throughput in some runtimes if the kernels are mature.
09:54 Sara Lim: So for our auditable model we might choose INT8 for determinism and run FP8 experiments in a separate performance track.
10:02 Priya Patel: Agreed. Security will prefer deterministic builds.
10:08 Maya Chen: Quick aside — have you tried toggling KV cache flush frequency? Maybe forcing a warmup phase reduces amplification.
10:18 Tom Nguyen: We hadn't. We'll try a 2-request warmup before traffic cutover.
10:25 Luis Romero: Also consider prefix-KV caching with deterministic ordering: reorder incoming batch by request ID so the cache writes are ordered. That trades a bit of scheduler flexibility for reproducibility.
10:38 Maya Chen: There was a mention earlier of kernel IDs — Luis can you explain what we'll log?
10:44 Luis Romero: We'll log the cuBLAS/cuDNN kernel ordinal and compile IDs where available, plus thread counts and math-mode flags. In Redwood's runtime we also log whether we used fused attention kernel A vs B and the block size. That helps correlate the run to a specific kernel behavior.
11:02 Arjun Patel: For on-prem runs we'll also pin CPU governor and disable frequency scaling to avoid timing nondeterminism.
11:10 Tom Nguyen: Makes sense.
11:18 (short cross-talk)
11:30 Maya Chen: Any final questions?
11:35 Rajesh Menon: From a compliance angle, if we provide deterministic artifacts and a record of the kernel versions and reproducible logs, that should satisfy the audit team.
11:46 Tom Nguyen: One practical ask — can Redwood provide a script to compare per-layer logits and produce a small visualization or failure summary so we don't dig manually?
11:55 Luis Romero: Yes, we'll include a diff tool that produces a ranked list of layers by max absolute diff and a small plot. We'll also include production-like traces for the failing case.
12:08 Sara Lim: And please include guidance on whether to prefer AWQ or GPTQ for long-sequence summarization workloads.
12:18 Luis Romero: We'll include recommendations: larger calibration sets, locked seeds, prefer GPTQ if you can afford the calibration time; AWQ with tuned outlier preservation if speed is needed.
12:30 Maya Chen: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll reconvene after the first repro runs.
12:35 (meeting ends)
crm_notes: Customer reported small regression after canary INT8 rollout. Team to run deterministic repro harness with pinned kernels. Audit-friendly artifacts requested.
